cards.title: Craig Faust
cards.sub: 1979 · TMI-2 control room operator, Metropolitan Edison
cards.body: One of four men on shift when TMI-2 tripped. Trained to react fast to a turbine trip, he was instead handed a cascade of alarms he could not rank. He later told the President's Commission he would have liked to have thrown away the alarm panel: it was not giving them any useful information.
cards.prompt: An operator was on shift at TMI-2 that morning and later testified about the alarm panel. Name him, and state what his testimony says about an alarm you cannot rank.
cards.answer: Craig Faust, a TMI-2 control room operator. He told the Commission he would have liked to throw the alarm panel away because it was giving no useful information — an unrankable alarm carries no information, so adding alarms subtracts signal.

cards.title: The stuck PORV
cards.sub: 28 March 1979 · Three Mile Island Unit 2, near Middletown, Pennsylvania
cards.body: Feedwater stopped at 4:00 a.m. The pressurizer relief valve opened as designed and was commanded shut thirteen seconds into the accident. It stayed open 2 hours and 22 minutes. About 32,000 gallons of coolant — over a third of the system — escaped in the first 100 minutes. The core was severely damaged.
cards.prompt: Give the price tag and the duration: how long was the TMI-2 relief valve open before anyone shut it, and what did the President's Commission estimate the accident's direct financial cost at?
cards.answer: 2 hours and 22 minutes. The Commission's best estimate of the accident's direct financial cost was $1 to $2 billion; the cleanup then ran on to 1993.

cards.title: Kemeny Report, Commission Finding A.3
cards.sub: October 1979 · President's Commission on the Accident at Three Mile Island
cards.body: The report you can still open. Finding A.3 states the indicator light showed only that the signal had been sent to close the PORV rather than the fact that the PORV remained open. The Task Force volume adds the wiring: the lamp read power applied to the actuation solenoid, not valve stem position.
cards.prompt: Which 1979 primary document is the source for 'the light showed only that the signal had been sent'? Name it, its chairman, and the electrical detail that explains why the lamp could not tell the truth.
cards.answer: The Report of the President's Commission on the Accident at Three Mile Island (the Kemeny Report), chaired by John G. Kemeny, October 1979. The lamp was wired to the actuation solenoid that carried the close command, not to the valve stem, so it reported intent and not position.

cards.title: Instrument the effect, not the command
cards.body: TMI shows why a good SLI is measured where the user is. 'Deploy job returned success', 'consumer process is up', 'CPU is fine' are all solenoid lamps: they report a command issued, not an outcome delivered. And 100 alarms with no ranking is worse than one: rank one signal, and page on burn rate.
cards.prompt: Your release alert fires on 'the deploy job returned success' and your queue alert fires on 'the consumer process is up'. Which TMI-2 component are you rebuilding, and what must each alert read instead?
cards.answer: The PORV indicator lamp — both alerts measure a command sent, not an effect delivered. Replace them with a user-visible signal: checkout success rate after the deploy, and consumer lag or messages actually delivered, alerted on burn rate against the SLO.
